Gaussian Study Guide

Gaussian probability connects uncertain voltage readings to receiver error rates. This guide develops the Gaussian distribution and Q function, binary decisions, averaging, and transformations, then applies them to filtered noise, envelopes, and sampled signals. Practical explanations accompany the mathematics; worked problems follow their relevant topics.

Gaussian Distribution and Q Function

Why we study a Gaussian distribution

A noisy receiver voltage can change every time it is measured, even when the transmitted symbol stays the same. A reading at one fixed instant is represented by a random variable. The complete uncertain waveform is a random process: each instant has a random variable, and one recorded waveform is a realization of that process.

Many small, approximately independent disturbances can combine into a nearly Gaussian voltage. This makes the Gaussian distribution useful for describing receiver noise and calculating the chance that a reading crosses a decision threshold. The central limit theorem explains this approximation; a mean and a variance alone do not prove that a variable is Gaussian.

The density and its parameters

Write

X∼𝒩(μX,σX2),σX>0.X\sim\mathcal N(\mu_X,\sigma_X^2),\qquad \sigma_X>0.

The first parameter is the mean; the second is the variance:

μX=E{X},σX2=E{(X−μX)2},σX=σX2.\mu_X=E\{X\},\qquad \sigma_X^2=E\{(X-\mu_X)^2\},\qquad \sigma_X=\sqrt{\sigma_X^2}.

The probability density is

fX(x)=12πσXexp[−(x−μX)22σX2],x∈ℝ.f_X(x)=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}\,\sigma_X} \exp\!\left[-\frac{(x-\mu_X)^2}{2\sigma_X^2}\right], \qquad x\in\mathbb R.

The mean locates the centre of the symmetric bell shape. The standard deviation measures its spread in the same units as the voltage. Increasing σX\sigma_X makes large deviations from the mean more likely. A density value is not a point probability: probabilities are areas under the curve.

P(a<X≤b)=∫abfX(x)dx,P(X=x)=0.P(a<X\le b)=\int_a^b f_X(x)\,dx,\qquad P(X=x)=0.

The mean-square value is

E{X2}=σX2+μX2.E\{X^2\}=\sigma_X^2+\mu_X^2.

Thus a zero-mean noise voltage can have nonzero mean-square value and deliver power.

Standardization

Instead of integrating a different Gaussian density for every mean and variance, measure the reading in standard deviations from its mean:

Z=X−μXσX∼𝒩(0,1).Z=\frac{X-\mu_X}{\sigma_X}\sim\mathcal N(0,1).

A threshold cc is therefore at the standardized distance (c−μX)/σX(c-\mu_X)/\sigma_X. This converts every Gaussian probability calculation into one involving the same standard normal curve.

The Q function

The Q function is the upper-tail area of the standard Gaussian density:

Q(z)=12π∫z∞e−u2/2du.Q(z)=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}}\int_z^\infty e^{-u^2/2}\,du.

Its symmetry gives

Q(0)=12,Q(−z)=1−Q(z).Q(0)=\frac12,\qquad Q(-z)=1-Q(z).

For X∼𝒩(μX,σX2)X\sim\mathcal N(\mu_X,\sigma_X^2),

P(X>c)=Q(c−μXσX),P(X>c)=Q\!\left(\frac{c-\mu_X}{\sigma_X}\right),

P(X≤c)=FX(c)=1−Q(c−μXσX).P(X\le c)=F_X(c) =1-Q\!\left(\frac{c-\mu_X}{\sigma_X}\right).

For an interval, subtract the two upper tails:

P(a<X≤b)=Q(a−μXσX)−Q(b−μXσX).P(a<X\le b) =Q\!\left(\frac{a-\mu_X}{\sigma_X}\right) -Q\!\left(\frac{b-\mu_X}{\sigma_X}\right).

For k≥0k\ge0, symmetry also gives

P(|X−μX|>kσX)=2Q(k),P(|X-\mu_X|>k\sigma_X)=2Q(k),

P(|X−μX|≤kσX)=1−2Q(k).P(|X-\mu_X|\le k\sigma_X)=1-2Q(k).

In a receiver, an error tail is the part of the voltage distribution lying beyond the wrong decision threshold. The Q function turns the threshold distance into that error probability. Larger positive distances give smaller tail areas.

Linear gains and voltage offsets change the Gaussian mean and spread; their distribution formulas are developed in the section on transformations.

Binary PAM Decision Error

A noisy amplitude decision

Binary pulse-amplitude modulation represents two symbols by opposite voltage levels. After receiving and sampling the signal, the receiver must decide which level was sent. Noise can move a positive level below the threshold or a negative level above it.

Let the transmitted symbol be

S∈{+A,−A},A>0,S\in\{+A,-A\},\qquad A>0,

with equal probabilities. Model the received sample as

Y=S+N,N∼𝒩(0,σN2),Y=S+N,\qquad N\sim\mathcal N(0,\sigma_N^2),

where the noise is independent of the transmitted symbol. For equal symbol probabilities and this symmetric noise model, the decision threshold is zero:

Ŝ={+A,Y≥0,−A,Y<0.\widehat S= \begin{cases} +A,&Y\ge0,\\ -A,&Y<0. \end{cases}

Conditional on the transmitted symbol, the received sample is Gaussian, centred at that symbol level. The two conditional distributions are separated by 2A2A and each has standard deviation σN\sigma_N. Without conditioning on the symbol, their equally weighted mixture is not generally a single Gaussian distribution.

Example: error probability for a zero-threshold receiver

Question

A binary PAM system transmits +A+A and −A-A with equal probabilities. The received sample is Y=S+NY=S+N, where N∼𝒩(0,σN2)N\sim\mathcal N(0,\sigma_N^2) is independent of SS. Find the conditional error probability for each symbol and the average error probability when the threshold is zero.

Solution

After transmitting +A+A,

Y∣(S=+A)∼𝒩(A,σN2).Y\mid(S=+A)\sim\mathcal N(A,\sigma_N^2).

An error occurs when the received value is negative:

P(error∣S=+A)=P(Y<0∣S=+A)=P(N<−A).P(\text{error}\mid S=+A) =P(Y<0\mid S=+A)=P(N<-A).

Standardizing the noise,

P(error∣S=+A)=P(NσN<−AσN)=1−Q(−AσN)=Q(AσN).P(\text{error}\mid S=+A) =P\!\left(\frac{N}{\sigma_N}<-\frac{A}{\sigma_N}\right) =1-Q\!\left(-\frac{A}{\sigma_N}\right) =Q\!\left(\frac{A}{\sigma_N}\right).

After transmitting −A-A, an error occurs on the positive side:

P(error∣S=−A)=P(N≥A)=Q(AσN).P(\text{error}\mid S=-A) =P(N\ge A)=Q\!\left(\frac{A}{\sigma_N}\right).

Weighting the two conditional probabilities by their equal priors,

Pe=12P(error∣S=+A)+12P(error∣S=−A)=Q(AσN).P_e=\frac12P(\text{error}\mid S=+A) +\frac12P(\text{error}\mid S=-A) =Q\!\left(\frac{A}{\sigma_N}\right).

The ratio A/σNA/\sigma_N measures how far the threshold lies from either symbol level in noise standard deviations. Increasing AA, or reducing the noise spread, makes it less likely that a sample crosses to the wrong side.

Central Limit Theorem and Averaging

Why sums often look Gaussian

A receiver disturbance may be the combined effect of many small contributions. Even if the individual contributions are not Gaussian, their sum can approach a Gaussian distribution. This explains why the Gaussian model is useful for noise; it does not make every kind of noise Gaussian.

Let X1,…,XnX_1,\ldots,X_n be independent, identically distributed variables with common finite mean μX\mu_X and finite positive variance σX2\sigma_X^2. For their sum,

Yn=∑k=1nXk,Y_n=\sum_{k=1}^{n}X_k,

E{Yn}=nμX,Var(Yn)=nσX2.E\{Y_n\}=n\mu_X,\qquad \operatorname{Var}(Y_n)=n\sigma_X^2.

The central limit theorem states that, as n→∞n\to\infty,

Zn=Yn−nμXσXnZ_n=\frac{Y_n-n\mu_X}{\sigma_X\sqrt n}

approaches the standard Gaussian distribution 𝒩(0,1)\mathcal N(0,1). Consequently, for sufficiently large nn in a suitable application,

Ynis approximately𝒩(nμX,nσX2).Y_n\ \text{is approximately}\ \mathcal N(n\mu_X,n\sigma_X^2).

This is an approximation for non-Gaussian summands. If the independent summands are already Gaussian, their sum is exactly Gaussian for every nn. The finite-variance and independence assumptions matter; the statement should not be applied simply because many terms are present.

Averaging repeated readings

Averaging is useful when the quantity of interest stays constant but independent measurement noise changes from reading to reading. The desired mean is preserved, while random fluctuations become smaller.

For the average

Mn=1n∑k=1nXk,M_n=\frac1n\sum_{k=1}^{n}X_k,

independence gives

E{Mn}=μX,Var(Mn)=σX2n,σMn=σXn.E\{M_n\}=\mu_X,\qquad \operatorname{Var}(M_n)=\frac{\sigma_X^2}{n},\qquad \sigma_{M_n}=\frac{\sigma_X}{\sqrt n}.

If the readings are independent Gaussian variables with a common law,

Mn∼𝒩(μX,σX2n)M_n\sim\mathcal N\!\left(\mu_X,\frac{\sigma_X^2}{n}\right)

exactly. For non-Gaussian independent identically distributed readings, the corresponding Gaussian shape is a central-limit approximation for large nn. Closely correlated readings do not generally provide the same variance reduction.

Example: Gaussian voltage and averaging

Question

A zero-mean Gaussian voltage has standard deviation 1010 V. Add a 55 V offset. Find the probability of a positive reading, then find the probability that the average of two independent readings is positive.

Solution

Let X∼𝒩(0,100)X\sim\mathcal N(0,100) and Y=X+5Y=X+5. The constant offset changes the mean and leaves the variance unchanged:

Y∼𝒩(5,100).Y\sim\mathcal N(5,100).

Standardizing the zero threshold,

P(Y>0)=Q(0−510)=1−Q(0.5)≈0.6915.P(Y>0)=Q\!\left(\frac{0-5}{10}\right) =1-Q(0.5)\approx0.6915.

For two independent readings, let

M=Y1+Y22.M=\frac{Y_1+Y_2}{2}.

Their average is exactly Gaussian:

E{M}=5,Var(M)=100+1004=50,E\{M\}=5,\qquad \operatorname{Var}(M)=\frac{100+100}{4}=50,

M∼𝒩(5,50).M\sim\mathcal N(5,50).

Therefore,

P(M>0)=Q(−550)=1−Q(550)≈0.7602.P(M>0)=Q\!\left(-\frac5{\sqrt{50}}\right) =1-Q\!\left(\frac5{\sqrt{50}}\right) \approx0.7602.

Averaging keeps the 55 V mean but reduces the standard deviation from 1010 V to 50\sqrt{50} V. The probability of identifying the positive level therefore increases. This calculation uses the exact Gaussian averaging law; no large-sample approximation is needed.

Transformations, Support, and Point Masses

Why a transformation changes the distribution

A receiver may amplify a noisy voltage, add a DC offset, rectify it, or limit its amplitude. If the input reading is the random variable XX, the device output is

Y=g(X).Y=g(X).

The transformation changes both the output values that can occur and the probabilities attached to them. An amplifier spreads or compresses the range; a rectifier can send many different input readings to the same output value. For this reason, transforming a density formula alone is not enough: the output support and any point masses must also be identified.

Start with the output CDF

The event Y≤yY\le y means that the input satisfies g(X)≤yg(X)\le y. Therefore,

FY(y)=P(Y≤y)=P(g(X)≤y).F_Y(y)=P(Y\le y)=P(g(X)\le y).

Find the input intervals satisfying the inequality, then add their probabilities. If XX has a density,

FY(y)=∫{x:g(x)≤y}fX(x)dx.F_Y(y)=\int_{\{x:g(x)\le y\}}f_X(x)\,dx.

The integral automatically ignores input values outside the support because fX(x)=0f_X(x)=0 there. The CDF method also works when part of the output law is discrete; an ordinary derivative describes only its continuous part.

A single inverse branch

Suppose XX has a density and gg is strictly monotone on its input support. With h(y)=g−1(y)h(y)=g^{-1}(y),

FY(y)={FX(h(y)),g increasing,1−FX(h(y)),g decreasing.F_Y(y)=\begin{cases} F_X(h(y)),&g\text{ increasing},\\ 1-F_X(h(y)),&g\text{ decreasing}. \end{cases}

Where the inverse is differentiable,

fY(y)=fX(h(y))|dh(y)dy|.\boxed{f_Y(y)=f_X(h(y))\left|\frac{dh(y)}{dy}\right|.}

The derivative accounts for the change in interval width. Compressing an input interval into a narrower output interval increases the density there while preserving its probability. Its absolute value keeps the density nonnegative when the transformation reverses the input order.

Use this expression only for output values reached by the supported input. For a bounded input interval [a,b][a,b] under Y=cX+dY=cX+d,

output interval={[ca+d,cb+d],c>0,[cb+d,ca+d],c<0.\text{output interval}=\begin{cases} [ca+d,\,cb+d],&c>0,\\ [cb+d,\,ca+d],&c<0. \end{cases}

The density is zero outside the admissible output range. A decreasing transformation swaps the two interval endpoints.

Several inverse branches

Different input values can produce the same output. If g(xi)=yg(x_i)=y on locally invertible continuous branches, each admissible root contributes:

fY,cont(y)=∑ifX(xi)|g′(xi)|,g′(xi)≠0.\boxed{f_{Y,\mathrm{cont}}(y)=\sum_i\frac{f_X(x_i)}{|g'(x_i)|},\qquad g'(x_i)\ne0.}

Include only roots belonging to the input support and the corresponding branch. Summing contributions is necessary because the output cannot distinguish which input branch produced the reading.

A square-law detector. Squaring a signed voltage makes its output nonnegative. For X∼𝒩(0,σX2)X\sim\mathcal N(0,\sigma_X^2) and Y=X2Y=X^2, an output y>0y>0 has two input roots, y\sqrt y and −y-\sqrt y:

fY(y)=fX(y)+fX(−y)2y=e−y/(2σX2)σX2πy,y>0.\begin{aligned} f_Y(y)&=\frac{f_X(\sqrt y)+f_X(-\sqrt y)}{2\sqrt y}\\ &=\frac{e^{-y/(2\sigma_X^2)}}{\sigma_X\sqrt{2\pi y}},\qquad y>0. \end{aligned}

The density is zero for y<0y<0. The output is not Gaussian: it has lost the sign of the input and cannot be negative. At y=0y=0, use the CDF or a limit rather than dividing by g′(0)=0g'(0)=0. Here the density grows without bound as y↓0y\downarrow0, but

P(Y=0)=P(X=0)=0.P(Y=0)=P(X=0)=0.

A zero derivative at an isolated input point does not, by itself, create a point mass.

Constant branches and point masses

A constant branch maps an entire set of input values to one output value y0y_0. Define

A={x:g(x)=y0}.A=\{x:g(x)=y_0\}.

Its total output mass is

P(Y=y0)=P(X∈A)=FY(y0)−FY(y0−).\boxed{P(Y=y_0)=P(X\in A)=F_Y(y_0)-F_Y(y_0^-).}

The notation FY(y0−)F_Y(y_0^-) denotes the left limit,

FY(y0−)=limy↑y0FY(y).F_Y(y_0^-)=\lim_{y\uparrow y_0}F_Y(y).

A CDF jump is a probability at one exact output value. For a density-bearing input, the mass can be evaluated as P(X∈A)=∫AfX(x)dxP(X\in A)=\int_A f_X(x)\,dx. It is positive only when the mapped set carries positive input probability. Retain the remaining continuous density separately; its integral need not equal one by itself.

If the output contains a continuous part and masses pkp_k at values yky_k, then

∫−∞∞fY,cont(y)dy+∑kpk=1.\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}f_{Y,\mathrm{cont}}(y)\,dy+\sum_k p_k=1.

The same law may be written using Dirac impulses:

fY(y)=fY,cont(y)+∑kpkδ(y−yk).f_Y(y)=f_{Y,\mathrm{cont}}(y)+\sum_k p_k\delta(y-y_k).

Here an impulse represents probability mass, rather than a finite density height.

A half-wave rectifier. For zero-mean Gaussian input and Y=max(X,0)Y=\max(X,0), every negative reading becomes zero, whereas positive readings remain unchanged. Consequently,

P(Y=0)=12,fY,cont(y)=fX(y),y>0.P(Y=0)=\frac12,\qquad f_{Y,\mathrm{cont}}(y)=f_X(y),\quad y>0.

The CDF is

FY(y)={0,y<0,FX(y),y≥0.F_Y(y)=\begin{cases} 0,&y<0,\\ F_X(y),&y\ge0. \end{cases}

It jumps from 00 to 1/21/2 at zero. The positive continuous part has probability 1/21/2; together, the mass and density account for all possible readings.

Amplifying and shifting Gaussian input

For X∼𝒩(μX,σX2)X\sim\mathcal N(\mu_X,\sigma_X^2) with σX>0\sigma_X>0, let

Y=cX+d,c≠0.Y=cX+d,\qquad c\ne0.

The inverse is x=(y−d)/cx=(y-d)/c, so

fY(y)=1|c|fX(y−dc)=12πc2σX2exp[−(y−cμX−d)22c2σX2],y∈ℝ.\begin{aligned} f_Y(y)&=\frac1{|c|}f_X\!\left(\frac{y-d}{c}\right)\\ &=\frac1{\sqrt{2\pi c^2\sigma_X^2}}\exp\!\left[-\frac{(y-c\mu_X-d)^2}{2c^2\sigma_X^2}\right],\qquad y\in\mathbb R. \end{aligned}

Therefore,

Y∼𝒩(cμX+d,c2σX2).\boxed{Y\sim\mathcal N(c\mu_X+d,\,c^2\sigma_X^2).}

The DC offset dd shifts the mean without changing the spread. The gain cc multiplies the standard deviation by |c||c| and the variance by c2c^2. A negative gain reverses the voltage polarity, but the variance remains nonnegative. The Gaussian support remains all of ℝ\mathbb R for every nonzero gain.

If c=0c=0, the output is always dd:

P(Y=d)=1,FY(y)={0,y<d,1,y≥d.P(Y=d)=1,\qquad F_Y(y)=\begin{cases}0,&y<d,\\1,&y\ge d.\end{cases}

This is a point mass, so the nonzero-gain density formula does not apply.

Worked Problems

A transformation producing both a point mass and a continuous density

Question

Let X∼𝒰[−2,2]X\sim\mathcal U[-2,2] and Y=g(X)Y=g(X), where g(x)={−1,−2≤x<0,2x/3,0≤x<3,2,x≥3.g(x)=\begin{cases}-1,&-2\leq x<0,\\2x/3,&0\leq x<3,\\2,&x\geq3.\end{cases} Find and sketch FX(x)F_X(x), fY(y)f_Y(y), and FY(y)F_Y(y).

Solution

Input distribution fX(x)=14𝟏(−2,2)(x),FX(x)={0,x<−2,(x+2)/4,−2≤x<2,1,x≥2. f_X(x)=\tfrac14\mathbf1_{(-2,2)}(x),\qquad \boxed{F_X(x)=\begin{cases}0,&x<-2,\\(x+2)/4,&-2\leq x<2,\\1,&x\geq2.\end{cases}}

Point mass and continuous density The input never reaches x=3x=3, so no mass occurs at y=2y=2. P(Y=−1)=P(X<0)=12,fY,cont(y)=fX(3y/2)|dxdy|=1432=38,0<y<43. \begin{aligned} P(Y=-1)&=P(X<0)=\frac12,\\ f_{Y,\mathrm{cont}}(y)&=f_X(3y/2)\left|\frac{dx}{dy}\right| =\frac14\frac32=\frac38,\qquad0<y<\frac43. \end{aligned} fY(y)=12δ(y+1)+38𝟏(0,4/3)(y)\boxed{f_Y(y)=\frac12\delta(y+1)+\frac38\mathbf1_{(0,4/3)}(y)} The delta term denotes a probability mass, rather than a finite density height.

Output CDF FY(y)={0,y<−1,12,−1≤y<0,12+38y,0≤y<43,1,y≥43. \boxed{F_Y(y)=\begin{cases} 0,&y<-1,\\ \tfrac12,&-1\leq y<0,\\ \tfrac12+\tfrac38y,&0\leq y<\tfrac43,\\ 1,&y\geq\tfrac43. \end{cases}} The CDF jumps by 1/21/2 at −1-1, then increases linearly from (0,1/2)(0,1/2) to (4/3,1)(4/3,1).

A continuous law with a point mass

Question

A random voltage has generalized density fX(x)=ku(x+7)e−1.72(x+7)+0.35δ(x−1),f_X(x)=k\,u(x+7)e^{-1.72(x+7)}+0.35\delta(x-1), where uu is the unit step and δ\delta is the Dirac impulse.

  • Determine the normalizing constant.
  • Obtain and sketch the CDF.
  • Calculate P(X≤0.5)P(X\le0.5), P(X>3)P(X>3), and P(0.5≤X≤3)P(0.5\le X\le3).

Solution

Continuous and discrete probability The impulse assigns P(X=1)=0.35P(X=1)=0.35; the continuous part must integrate to 0.650.65. 1=k∫−7∞e−1.72(x+7)dx+0.35=k1.72+0.35.1=k\int_{-7}^{\infty}e^{-1.72(x+7)}\,dx+0.35 =\frac{k}{1.72}+0.35. k=1.72(0.65)=1.118.\boxed{k=1.72(0.65)=1.118.}

Cumulative distribution FX(x)={0,x<−7,0.65[1−e−1.72(x+7)],−7≤x<1,0.65[1−e−1.72(x+7)]+0.35,x≥1.\boxed{F_X(x)=\begin{cases} 0,&x<-7,\\ 0.65[1-e^{-1.72(x+7)}],&-7\le x<1,\\ 0.65[1-e^{-1.72(x+7)}]+0.35,&x\ge1. \end{cases}} The CDF rises from zero at −7-7, jumps by 0.350.35 at 11, and approaches one asymptotically.

Requested probabilities There are no point masses at 0.50.5 or 33. P(X≤0.5)=0.65(1−e−12.9)≈0.6499983763.\boxed{P(X\le0.5)=0.65(1-e^{-12.9})\approx0.6499983763.} P(X>3)=0.65e−17.2≈2.20317×10−8.\boxed{P(X>3)=0.65e^{-17.2}\approx2.20317\times10^{-8}.} P(0.5≤X≤3)=FX(3)−FX(0.5)=0.35+0.65(e−12.9−e−17.2).\begin{aligned} P(0.5\le X\le3)&=F_X(3)-F_X(0.5)\\ &=0.35+0.65(e^{-12.9}-e^{-17.2}). \end{aligned} P(0.5≤X≤3)≈0.3500016017.\boxed{P(0.5\le X\le3)\approx0.3500016017.}

Gaussian Variables and Linear Filtering

A receiver adds, subtracts, and filters voltages. These operations change the noise power, but Gaussian inputs remain Gaussian under linear processing when the inputs are jointly Gaussian. This lets us predict a receiver’s output distribution without predicting its particular noise waveform.

Linear combinations

For jointly Gaussian variables, any linear combination is Gaussian. With real constants aia_i,

Y=∑iaiXi+d,Y=\sum_i a_iX_i+d,

μY=∑iaiμi+d,σY2=∑i∑jaiajCov(Xi,Xj).\mu_Y=\sum_i a_i\mu_i+d,\qquad \sigma_Y^2=\sum_i\sum_j a_ia_j\operatorname{Cov}(X_i,X_j).

For independent Gaussian inputs, this reduces to

σY2=∑iai2σi2.\boxed{\sigma_Y^2=\sum_i a_i^2\sigma_i^2}.

In particular, independent equal-variance noise branches satisfy

X1,X2∼𝒩(0,σb2)⇒X1−X2∼𝒩(0,2σb2).X_1,X_2\sim\mathcal N(0,\sigma_b^2) \quad\Longrightarrow\quad X_1-X_2\sim\mathcal N(0,2\sigma_b^2).

For a jointly Gaussian pair, zero covariance implies independence. Having two Gaussian marginal distributions alone does not establish joint Gaussianity. Independent variables have the product joint density

fX1,X2(x1,x2)=fX1(x1)fX2(x2).f_{X_1,X_2}(x_1,x_2)=f_{X_1}(x_1)f_{X_2}(x_2).

A Gaussian process is a family of possible waveforms

At a fixed time, X(t)X(t) is a random variable; over time, it is a random process. One measured voltage trace is one realization. A Gaussian process has jointly Gaussian values at every finite collection of sampling times, so its mean and covariance determine these finite-dimensional distributions.

A noise waveform can be Gaussian while adjacent samples are correlated. Gaussian describes amplitude statistics; white describes a flat power spectrum. These properties answer different questions.

The effect of a linear filter

For a real WSS input and a deterministic real LTI filter,

Y(t)=h(t)*X(t),μY=μXH(0).Y(t)=h(t)*X(t),\qquad \mu_Y=\mu_XH(0).

Whenever the output has a finite second moment, a Gaussian input gives a Gaussian output. The filter changes its spectrum according to

SY(f)=|H(f)|2SX(f).\boxed{S_Y(f)=|H(f)|^2S_X(f)}.

The autocorrelation and mean-square value follow from

RY(τ)=∫−∞∞SY(f)ej2πfτdf,R_Y(\tau)=\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}S_Y(f)e^{j2\pi f\tau}\,df,

PY=RY(0)=∫−∞∞SY(f)df,σY2=PY−μY2.P_Y=R_Y(0)=\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}S_Y(f)\,df, \qquad \sigma_Y^2=P_Y-\mu_Y^2.

Using the convention RXY(τ)=E{X(t+τ)Y(t)}R_{XY}(\tau)=E\{X(t+\tau)Y(t)\},

SXY(f)=SX(f)H*(f),SYX(f)=SX(f)H(f).S_{XY}(f)=S_X(f)H^*(f),\qquad S_{YX}(f)=S_X(f)H(f).

The output spectrum describes the admitted noise power; the cross spectrum also retains the filter’s phase.

Gaussian white noise after filtering

For zero-mean white Gaussian input with two-sided PSD N0/2N_0/2,

SY(f)=N02|H(f)|2,S_Y(f)=\frac{N_0}{2}|H(f)|^2,

σY2=N02∫−∞∞|H(f)|2df=N02∫−∞∞|h(t)|2dt.\boxed{\sigma_Y^2=\frac{N_0}{2}\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}|H(f)|^2df =\frac{N_0}{2}\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}|h(t)|^2dt}.

Thus the filter’s energy determines the variance of each output sample. The ideal unfiltered white-noise model has infinite total power; a finite-energy filter makes the output variance finite. Filtering generally makes the noise colored while preserving Gaussianity.

For measurement over a band |f|≤B|f|\leq B,

PY,B=∫−BBSY(f)df.P_{Y,B}=\int_{-B}^{B}S_Y(f)\,df.

This band power differs from the total output power unless the filter rejects every frequency outside the measurement band.

RC noise filtering

An RC low-pass filter smooths rapid voltage fluctuations. For RC>0RC>0,

H(f)=11+j2πRCf,H(f)=\frac{1}{1+j2\pi RCf},

SY(f)=N0/21+(2πRCf)2,RY(τ)=N04RCe−|τ|/(RC).S_Y(f)=\frac{N_0/2}{1+(2\pi RCf)^2},\qquad R_Y(\tau)=\frac{N_0}{4RC}e^{-|\tau|/(RC)}.

Therefore each fixed-time output value has distribution

Y(t)∼𝒩(0,N04RC).\boxed{Y(t)\sim\mathcal N\!\left(0,\frac{N_0}{4RC}\right)}.

Increasing RCRC reduces the output noise variance and increases the time over which samples remain correlated.

Worked Problems

Independent Gaussian branches and an estimation-error network

Question

Independent Gaussian white-noise processes W1(t)W_1(t) and W2(t)W_2(t) satisfy RWi(τ)=η2δ(τ).R_{W_i}(\tau)=\frac{\eta}{2}\delta(\tau). Identical real LTI filters h(t)h(t) produce N1(t)N_1(t) and N2(t)N_2(t). Define N=N1−N2,ε=N1−ho*N.N=N_1-N_2,\qquad \varepsilon=N_1-h_o*N. Find:

  • The density of NN and the joint density of N1,N2N_1,N_2 at a fixed time.
  • P(N>−1)P(N>-1).
  • A simplified expression for ε\varepsilon.

Solution

Branch statistics Assume η>0\eta>0 and 0<Eh<∞0<E_h<\infty. Eh=∫−∞∞|h(u)|2du,σb2=ηEh2,SNi(f)=η2|H(f)|2. E_h=\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}|h(u)|^2du,\qquad \sigma_b^2=\frac{\eta E_h}{2},\qquad S_{N_i}(f)=\frac{\eta}{2}|H(f)|^2. The branch outputs are independent, zero-mean Gaussian processes.

Densities and probability N∼𝒩(0,ηEh).N\sim\mathcal N(0,\eta E_h). fN(n)=e−n2/(2ηEh)2πηEh \boxed{f_N(n)=\frac{e^{-n^2/(2\eta E_h)}}{\sqrt{2\pi\eta E_h}}} fN1N2(n1,n2)=12πσb2exp[−n12+n222σb2] \boxed{f_{N_1N_2}(n_1,n_2)=\frac{1}{2\pi\sigma_b^2} \exp\left[-\frac{n_1^2+n_2^2}{2\sigma_b^2}\right]} P(N>−1)=1−Q(1ηEh)\boxed{P(N>-1)=1-Q\left(\frac1{\sqrt{\eta E_h}}\right)} A numerical probability requires ηEh\eta E_h.

Error network ε=(δ−ho)*N1+ho*N2\boxed{\varepsilon=(\delta-h_o)*N_1+h_o*N_2} Sε(f)=η2|H(f)|2(|1−Ho(f)|2+|Ho(f)|2). S_\varepsilon(f)=\frac{\eta}{2}|H(f)|^2 \left(|1-H_o(f)|^2+|H_o(f)|^2\right). Without a specified HoH_o, this is the general result. For minimum mean-square estimation, Ho=SN1NSN=12,ho=12δ, H_o=\frac{S_{N_1N}}{S_N}=\frac12,\qquad h_o=\tfrac12\delta, ε=N1+N22,Var(ε)=ηEh4\boxed{\varepsilon=\frac{N_1+N_2}{2},\qquad \operatorname{Var}(\varepsilon)=\frac{\eta E_h}{4}} If ηEh=0\eta E_h=0, the outputs vanish in mean square, the joint law is a point mass at the origin, and P(N>−1)=1P(N>-1)=1.

A Gaussian input through a first-order low-pass filter

Question

A zero-mean white Gaussian input has SX(f)=η/2S_X(f)=\eta/2 and drives a filter with h(t)=e−tu(t)h(t)=e^{-t}u(t).

Determine:

  • The output PSD, autocorrelation and mean-square value.
  • The input and output powers in the band |f|≤B|f|\le B, with positive low-pass edge B=103HzB=10^3\ \mathrm{Hz}.
  • The percentage of total output power within that band and the output-to-input power percentage within the same band.

Solution

Frequency response and output PSD

H(f)=∫0∞e−te−j2πftdt=11+j2πf,SY(f)=η2|H(f)|2. \begin{aligned} H(f)&=\int_0^\infty e^{-t}e^{-j2\pi ft}\,dt =\frac{1}{1+j2\pi f},\\ S_Y(f)&=\frac{\eta}{2}|H(f)|^2. \end{aligned}

Therefore,

SY(f)=η2[1+(2πf)2]. \boxed{S_Y(f)=\frac{\eta}{2[1+(2\pi f)^2]}}.

Autocorrelation and mean square

The exponential Fourier pair gives

RY(τ)=η4e−|τ|,E{Y2(t)}=PY,total=η4. \boxed{R_Y(\tau)=\frac{\eta}{4}e^{-|\tau|}}, \qquad \boxed{E\{Y^2(t)\}=P_{Y,\mathrm{total}}=\frac{\eta}{4}}.

Powers in the measurement band

PX,B=∫−BBη2df=ηB=1000η,PY,B=η2∫−BBdf1+(2πf)2=η2πtan−1(2πB). \begin{aligned} P_{X,B}&=\int_{-B}^{B}\frac{\eta}{2}\,df =\boxed{\eta B=1000\eta},\\ P_{Y,B}&=\frac{\eta}{2}\int_{-B}^{B}\frac{df}{1+(2\pi f)^2} =\boxed{\frac{\eta}{2\pi}\tan^{-1}(2\pi B)}. \end{aligned}

Power percentages

At B=103HzB=10^3\ \mathrm{Hz},

100PY,BPY,total=1002πtan−1(2πB)≈99.9899%, \boxed{100\frac{P_{Y,B}}{P_{Y,\mathrm{total}}} =100\frac{2}{\pi}\tan^{-1}(2\pi B) \approx99.9899\%},

100PY,BPX,B=100tan−1(2πB)2πB≈0.0249975%. \boxed{100\frac{P_{Y,B}}{P_{X,B}} =100\frac{\tan^{-1}(2\pi B)}{2\pi B} \approx0.0249975\%}.

The first ratio measures how much of the total filtered noise lies in the measurement band; the second compares output and input powers over that same band.

Gaussian Quadratures, Envelope, and Phase

Radio noise near a carrier can be described by two slowly varying components. These are the noise coordinates along cosine and sine carrier references. Their geometry shows how noise changes a received carrier’s strength and phase.

In-phase and quadrature components

Write zero-mean stationary Gaussian narrowband noise as

n(t)=nc(t)cos(2πfct)−ns(t)sin(2πfct).n(t)=n_c(t)\cos(2\pi f_ct)-n_s(t)\sin(2\pi f_ct).

At a fixed time, its standard quadrature components are jointly Gaussian with equal variance and zero covariance:

nc,ns∼𝒩(0,σ2),E{ncns}=0.n_c,n_s\sim\mathcal N(0,\sigma^2),\qquad E\{n_cn_s\}=0.

They are therefore independent at that time. Their common variance equals the bandpass noise power,

σ2=Pn=∫−∞∞Sn(f)df,\sigma^2=P_n=\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}S_n(f)df,

and their same-time joint density is

fnc,ns(u,v)=12πσ2exp[−u2+v22σ2].f_{n_c,n_s}(u,v)=\frac{1}{2\pi\sigma^2} \exp\!\left[-\frac{u^2+v^2}{2\sigma^2}\right].

The equal variances make this density circularly symmetric in the (u,v)(u,v) plane. Same-time independence does not imply independence between components at different times; carrier-centered spectral symmetry supplies the stronger process independence.

From Gaussian coordinates to envelope and phase

Define

R=nc2+ns2,Θ=atan2(ns,nc).R=\sqrt{n_c^2+n_s^2},\qquad \Theta=\operatorname{atan2}(n_s,n_c).

Then

n(t)=R(t)cos[2πfct+Θ(t)].n(t)=R(t)\cos[2\pi f_ct+\Theta(t)].

The envelope is a nonnegative magnitude, so its support is r≥0r\geq0. Transforming u=rcosθu=r\cos\theta, v=rsinθv=r\sin\theta contributes the Jacobian magnitude rr:

fR,Θ(r,θ)=r2πσ2e−r2/(2σ2),r≥0,−π<θ≤π.f_{R,\Theta}(r,\theta)=\frac{r}{2\pi\sigma^2} e^{-r^2/(2\sigma^2)},\qquad r\geq0,\quad-\pi<\theta\leq\pi.

The density factors into

fR(r)=rσ2e−r2/(2σ2),r≥0,\boxed{f_R(r)=\frac{r}{\sigma^2}e^{-r^2/(2\sigma^2)},\quad r\geq0},

fΘ(θ)=12π,−π<θ≤π.\boxed{f_\Theta(\theta)=\frac1{2\pi},\quad-\pi<\theta\leq\pi}.

Thus the noise envelope is Rayleigh, its phase is uniform, and they are independent at a fixed time. There is no preferred phase direction because the zero-mean Gaussian coordinate density is circularly symmetric. Although the coordinates are Gaussian, their nonnegative magnitude is not Gaussian.

Useful envelope moments are

E{R}=σπ2,E{R2}=2σ2,E\{R\}=\sigma\sqrt{\frac\pi2},\qquad E\{R^2\}=2\sigma^2,

Var(R)=(2−π2)σ2.\operatorname{Var}(R)=\left(2-\frac\pi2\right)\sigma^2.

Adding a deterministic carrier

For x(t)=Acos(2πfct)x(t)=A\cos(2\pi f_ct), addition of the noise gives

y(t)=[A+nc(t)]cos(2πfct)−ns(t)sin(2πfct).y(t)=[A+n_c(t)]\cos(2\pi f_ct)-n_s(t)\sin(2\pi f_ct).

Matching this with ρ(t)cos[2πfct+θ(t)]\rho(t)\cos[2\pi f_ct+\theta(t)] yields

ρcosθ=A+nc,ρsinθ=ns,\rho\cos\theta=A+n_c,\qquad \rho\sin\theta=n_s,

ρ=(A+nc)2+ns2,θ=atan2(ns,A+nc).\boxed{\rho=\sqrt{(A+n_c)^2+n_s^2}},\qquad \boxed{\theta=\operatorname{atan2}(n_s,A+n_c)}.

The carrier shifts the Gaussian coordinate cloud by AA along the in-phase axis. The envelope is no longer Rayleigh for a nonzero carrier, and the phase need not be uniform. The two-argument arctangent selects the correct quadrant; phase is immaterial when the envelope vanishes.

Worked Problems

Envelope and phase of a carrier with narrowband noise

Question

A carrier x(t)=Acos(2πfct)x(t)=A\cos(2\pi f_ct) is added to narrowband noise n(t)=nc(t)cos(2πfct)−ns(t)sin(2πfct). n(t)=n_c(t)\cos(2\pi f_ct)-n_s(t)\sin(2\pi f_ct). Express y(t)=x(t)+n(t)y(t)=x(t)+n(t) in the form y(t)=ρ(t)cos[2πfct+θ(t)]. y(t)=\rho(t)\cos[2\pi f_ct+\theta(t)].

Solution

Combine the quadrature components

y(t)=[A+nc(t)]cos(2πfct)−ns(t)sin(2πfct). y(t)=[A+n_c(t)]\cos(2\pi f_ct)-n_s(t)\sin(2\pi f_ct).

Match the envelope–phase coefficients

Expanding ρ(t)cos[2πfct+θ(t)]\rho(t)\cos[2\pi f_ct+\theta(t)] gives

ρ(t)cosθ(t)=A+nc(t),ρ(t)sinθ(t)=ns(t). \begin{aligned} \rho(t)\cos\theta(t)&=A+n_c(t),\\ \rho(t)\sin\theta(t)&=n_s(t). \end{aligned}

Hence

ρ(t)=[A+nc(t)]2+ns2(t), \boxed{\rho(t)=\sqrt{[A+n_c(t)]^2+n_s^2(t)}},

θ(t)=atan2(ns(t),A+nc(t)). \boxed{\theta(t)=\operatorname{atan2}\big(n_s(t),A+n_c(t)\big)}.

The two-argument arctangent selects the correct quadrant. When ρ(t)=0\rho(t)=0, phase may be assigned arbitrarily.

Sampled Gaussian Signals and Prediction

A digital receiver measures an analogue waveform at successive instants. If nearby samples are correlated, the previous samples contain information about the next one. A predictor removes this predictable part, leaving a smaller error to encode or quantize.

From a spectrum to sampled statistics

For a real WSS Gaussian process sampled every TsT_s seconds,

X[n]=X(nTs),Ts=1fs,X[n]=X(nT_s),\qquad T_s=\frac1{f_s},

RX(τ)=∫−∞∞SX(f)ej2πfτdf,rX[k]=RX(kTs).R_X(\tau)=\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}S_X(f)e^{j2\pi f\tau}\,df, \qquad r_X[k]=R_X(kT_s).

For zero mean,

Cov(X[i],X[j])=rX[i−j].\operatorname{Cov}(X[i],X[j])=r_X[i-j].

These quantities specify the joint Gaussian law of a sample vector. A spectrum does not supply the actual amplitudes of one measured realization.

Minimum mean-square prediction

For rX[0]>0r_X[0]>0, consider a one-tap predictor

X̂[n]=aX[n−1],D[n]=X[n]−aX[n−1].\widehat X[n]=aX[n-1],\qquad D[n]=X[n]-aX[n-1].

The best coefficient makes the error orthogonal to the available sample:

E{D[n]X[n−1]}=rX[1]−arX[0]=0.E\{D[n]X[n-1]\}=r_X[1]-ar_X[0]=0.

Hence

a=rX[1]rX[0],σD2=rX[0]−rX2[1]rX[0].\boxed{a=\frac{r_X[1]}{r_X[0]}},\qquad \boxed{\sigma_D^2=r_X[0]-\frac{r_X^2[1]}{r_X[0]}}.

For an MM-tap predictor, the corresponding orthogonality equations are

∑j=1MajrX[k−j]=rX[k],k=1,…,M.\sum_{j=1}^{M}a_jr_X[k-j]=r_X[k],\qquad k=1,\ldots,M.

The zero covariance between the optimum error and the past samples also gives independence when the variables are jointly Gaussian. This is why the Gaussian assumption simplifies the prediction problem.

Exponential correlation

If

rX[k]=σX2ρ|k|,|ρ|<1,r_X[k]=\sigma_X^2\rho^{|k|},\qquad |\rho|<1,

the optimum predictor from any finite number of past samples has

a1=ρ,a2=a3=⋯=0,\boxed{a_1=\rho,\qquad a_2=a_3=\cdots=0},

X[n]=ρX[n−1]+D[n],σD2=σX2(1−ρ2).X[n]=\rho X[n-1]+D[n],\qquad \boxed{\sigma_D^2=\sigma_X^2(1-\rho^2)}.

The innovations D[n]D[n] are independent zero-mean Gaussian variables. The first previous sample already contains the predictive information provided by the more distant past under this covariance model.

Quantizing the prediction error

Use the stated Gaussian quantization model

Pq=2σD2Q2.P_q=\frac{2\sigma_D^2}{Q^2}.

Here QQ is the number of levels. This is a specified model for the exercise, rather than a formula for every Gaussian quantizer. To meet a maximum allowed noise power,

Q≥2σD2Pq,max,Qmin=⌈2σD2Pq,max⌉.Q\geq\sqrt{\frac{2\sigma_D^2}{P_{q,\max}}},\qquad \boxed{Q_{\min}=\left\lceil\sqrt{\frac{2\sigma_D^2}{P_{q,\max}}}\right\rceil}.

For binary coding,

b=⌈log2Qmin⌉,Qimplemented=2b.b=\lceil\log_2Q_{\min}\rceil,\qquad Q_{\mathrm{implemented}}=2^b.

A smaller prediction-error variance needs fewer levels for the same distortion limit. The inequality must be checked before rounding: a value just above an integer requires the next integer.

Worked Problems

Prediction of a sampled Gaussian process

Question

A zero-mean Gaussian process has SX(f)=161+(16πf)2,fs=1Hz.S_X(f)=\frac{16}{1+(16\pi f)^2},\qquad f_s=1\,\mathrm{Hz}. A differential quantizer subtracts the predictor X̂[n]=a1X[n−1]+a2X[n−2]+a3X[n−3].\widehat X[n]=a_1X[n-1]+a_2X[n-2]+a_3X[n-3]. For a Gaussian input of variance σ2\sigma^2 and QQ quantization levels, the quantization-noise power is 2σ2/Q22\sigma^2/Q^2.

  • Find the number of levels required for noise power at most 4.32×10−44.32\times10^{-4}.
  • Determine the sampled-process values at Ts,2Ts,3Ts,4TsT_s,2T_s,3T_s,4T_s.

Solution

Correlation and optimum prediction Assume minimum mean-square prediction. With Ts=1sT_s=1\,\mathrm s, RX(τ)=e−|τ|/8,ρ=e−1/8=0.882496903,rX[m]=ρ|m|. R_X(\tau)=e^{-|\tau|/8},\qquad \rho=e^{-1/8}=0.882496903,\qquad r_X[m]=\rho^{|m|}. [1ρρ2ρ1ρρ2ρ1][a1a2a3]=[ρρ2ρ3]⇒a1=ρ,a2=a3=0. \begin{bmatrix}1&\rho&\rho^2\\\rho&1&\rho\\\rho^2&\rho&1\end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix}a_1\\a_2\\a_3\end{bmatrix} =\begin{bmatrix}\rho\\\rho^2\\\rho^3\end{bmatrix} \quad\Longrightarrow\quad \boxed{a_1=\rho,\quad a_2=a_3=0}. X[n]=ρX[n−1]+D[n],σD2=1−e−1/4=0.221199217. X[n]=\rho X[n-1]+D[n],\qquad \boxed{\sigma_D^2=1-e^{-1/4}=0.221199217}.

Quantization levels 2σD2Q2≤4.32×10−4,Q≥2(1−e−1/4)4.32×10−4=32.0011007. \begin{aligned} \frac{2\sigma_D^2}{Q^2}&\leq4.32\times10^{-4},\\ Q&\geq\sqrt{\frac{2(1-e^{-1/4})}{4.32\times10^{-4}}}=32.0011007. \end{aligned} Qmin=33\boxed{Q_{\min}=33} For Q=32Q=32, Pq=4.3202972×10−4P_q=4.3202972\times10^{-4}, just above the bound. If QQ must be a power of two, Q=64,b=6\boxed{Q=64,\ b=6}.

Sample statistics A PSD does not determine individual sample amplitudes. The available results are E{X[i]}=0,Var(X[i])=1,Cov(X[i],X[j])=ρ|i−j|,i,j∈{1,2,3,4}. E\{X[i]\}=0,\qquad \operatorname{Var}(X[i])=1,\qquad \operatorname{Cov}(X[i],X[j])=\rho^{|i-j|},\quad i,j\in\{1,2,3,4\}. Given X[0]X[0] and independent Gaussian innovations D[k]D[k], actual samples follow from X[n]=ρnX[0]+∑k=1nρn−kD[k].X[n]=\rho^nX[0]+\sum_{k=1}^{n}\rho^{n-k}D[k]. The corresponding autocorrelation samples are RX(Ts)=0.882497,RX(2Ts)=0.778801,RX(3Ts)=0.687289,RX(4Ts)=0.606531. \begin{aligned} R_X(T_s)&=0.882497,&R_X(2T_s)&=0.778801,\\ R_X(3T_s)&=0.687289,&R_X(4T_s)&=0.606531. \end{aligned}

Matched Filtering and Binary Decisions

A receiver often has to recognize a known pulse buried in noise. A matched filter combines the pulse contributions so they reinforce one another at the sampling instant. The remaining noise at that instant is Gaussian, so its probability of crossing the decision threshold is evaluated with the QQ function.

Matching a known pulse

For a pulse s(t)s(t) of energy

Es=∫−∞∞|s(t)|2dt,E_s=\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}|s(t)|^2dt,

and zero-mean additive white Gaussian noise with two-sided PSD N0/2N_0/2, the matched impulse response is

h(t)=Ks*(T−t),K≠0.\boxed{h(t)=Ks^*(T-t)},\qquad K\ne0.

For a real pulse and real gain,

Rs(τ)=∫−∞∞s(u+τ)s(u)du,R_s(\tau)=\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}s(u+\tau)s(u)du,

ys(t)=KRs(t−T),ys(T)=KEs.y_s(t)=KR_s(t-T),\qquad y_s(T)=KE_s.

Time reversal aligns the entire pulse with the filter at t=Tt=T. Its output noise variance is

σn,o2=N02|K|2Es,\sigma_{n,o}^2=\frac{N_0}{2}|K|^2E_s,

so

SNRmax=|KEs|2(N0/2)|K|2Es=2EsN0.\boxed{\mathrm{SNR}_{\max} =\frac{|K E_s|^2}{(N_0/2)|K|^2E_s} =\frac{2E_s}{N_0}}.

Changing KK scales both signal and noise, leaving SNR unchanged. The matched filter maximizes the sampling-instant SNR for the given pulse in white noise; it does not remove the noise.

Gaussian tails become decision errors

For equiprobable bits in coherent, undistorted AWGN reception, the receiver compares a noisy decision statistic with its threshold. An error occurs when the Gaussian noise moves that statistic to the wrong side.

For binary PSK, whose two signals are antipodal,

Pe,BPSK=Q(2EbN0).\boxed{P_{e,\mathrm{BPSK}}=Q\!\left(\sqrt{\frac{2E_b}{N_0}}\right)}.

For coherent binary FSK with orthogonal equal-energy signals,

Pe,BFSK=Q(EbN0).\boxed{P_{e,\mathrm{BFSK}}=Q\!\left(\sqrt{\frac{E_b}{N_0}}\right)}.

For a passband sinusoid of amplitude AA over a bit interval TbT_b, with the usual carrier-cycle energy approximation,

Tb=1Rb,Eb≃A2Tb2.T_b=\frac1{R_b},\qquad E_b\simeq\frac{A^2T_b}{2}.

Here RbR_b is the bit rate. Orthogonal FSK requires the appropriate tone spacing over the observation interval; ΔfTb=1\Delta fT_b=1 is a suitable envelope-model spacing. Coherent reception assumes the carrier reference needed for these formulas is available.

Increasing bit energy relative to noise density makes a threshold crossing less likely. At fixed signal power, increasing the bit rate reduces energy per bit and can therefore increase the error probability.

Rate and pulse-shaping bandwidth

The maximum bit rate cannot be inferred from channel bandwidth without a signaling and pulse-shaping assumption. For binary PSK with raised-cosine roll-off α\alpha and positive-frequency lobe width BB,

B=(1+α)Rb,Rb≤B1+α.B=(1+\alpha)R_b,\qquad R_b\leq\frac{B}{1+\alpha}.

Ideal zero roll-off gives Rb≤BR_b\leq B. Rectangular pulses instead give the first-null approximation

B≃2Rb.B\simeq2R_b.

Their sidelobes extend beyond this interval. A filter that truncates these sidelobes can distort the waveform, so first-null bandwidth is an approximation rather than an exact distortion-free rate bound.

Worked Problems

Matched filtering of a flat-topped pulse

Question

The pulse is s(t)={1,0≤t<1,2−t,1≤t<2,0,otherwise.s(t)=\begin{cases}1,&0\leq t<1,\\2-t,&1\leq t<2,\\0,&\text{otherwise}.\end{cases} The two-sided AWGN PSD is (2/3)×10−3W/Hz(2/3)\times10^{-3}\,\mathrm{W/Hz}.

  • Find and sketch a matched-filter impulse response and its signal output.
  • Find the time and magnitude of the maximum output.
  • Determine the maximum output SNR.

Solution

Matched impulse response Choose unit gain and sampling time T=2T=2. h(t)=s(2−t)={t,0<t≤1,1,1<t≤2,0,otherwise. \boxed{h(t)=s(2-t)=\begin{cases}t,&0<t\leq1,\\1,&1<t\leq2,\\0,&\text{otherwise}.\end{cases}}

R_s(a)=\int_a^1du+\int_1^{1+a}(2-u)du +\int_{1+a}^2(2-u)(2-u+a)du. For 1<a≤21<a\leq2, Rs(a)=∫a2(2−u)duR_s(a)=\int_a^2(2-u)du. Coherent binary FSK and PSK error probabilities

Question

A unity-gain channel passes 500≤|f|≤1500Hz500\leq|f|\leq1500\,\mathrm{Hz} and rejects all other frequencies. The amplitude-to-noise ratio is A2/η=8000A^2/\eta=8000.

  • Find the coherent binary FSK error probability at 200bit/s200\,\mathrm{bit/s} with tones at 1070 and 1270 Hz.
  • Determine the fastest PSK rate and its coherent error probability.

Solution

Assume equiprobable bits, two-sided AWGN PSD η/2=N0/2\eta/2=N_0/2, sinusoid amplitude AA, and negligible distortion of the shaped signals.

Coherent FSK Tb=1/200=0.005s,(f2−f1)Tb=200(0.005)=1,EbN0≃A2Tb2η=80000.0052=20. \begin{aligned} T_b&=1/200=0.005\,\mathrm s,\\ (f_2-f_1)T_b&=200(0.005)=1,\\ \frac{E_b}{N_0}&\simeq\frac{A^2T_b}{2\eta}=8000\frac{0.005}{2}=20. \end{aligned} The spacing satisfies envelope-model orthogonality. Pe,FSK=Q(20)=3.8721×10−6\boxed{P_{e,\mathrm{FSK}}=Q(\sqrt{20})=3.8721\times10^{-6}}

Binary PSK with ideal Nyquist shaping A maximum rate requires a pulse-shaping and modulation-order assumption. For binary PSK with zero roll-off, the positive-lobe width B=1000HzB=1000\,\mathrm{Hz} equals RbR_b. Rb,max=1000bit/s\boxed{R_{b,\max}=1000\,\mathrm{bit/s}} EbN0=A22ηRb=4,\frac{E_b}{N_0}=\frac{A^2}{2\eta R_b}=4, Pe,BPSK=Q(8)=2.33887×10−3\boxed{P_{e,\mathrm{BPSK}}=Q(\sqrt8)=2.33887\times10^{-3}} For raised-cosine roll-off α\alpha, Rb,max=B/(1+α)R_{b,\max}=B/(1+\alpha).

Rectangular-pulse bandwidth approximation Using the first-null approximation B≃2RbB\simeq2R_b, Rb≃500bit/s,Eb/N0=8,R_b\simeq500\,\mathrm{bit/s},\qquad E_b/N_0=8, Pe≃Q(4)=3.16712×10−5\boxed{P_e\simeq Q(4)=3.16712\times10^{-5}} This assumes undistorted coherent detection. A brick-wall channel truncates rectangular-pulse sidelobes, so the approximation is not an exact distortion analysis. Higher-order PSK requires a specified order.
